enrichment_sources: MIABIS Core 3.0 (32 attributes, modular; MIABIS 2.0 Core had 22) plus the MIABIS individual-level extension, whose sample attributes were drawn from ISBER's SPREC - use these as the field vocabulary rather than inventing one
Ontologies: UBERON (anatomy), NCIt/ORDO (disease)
compliance_notes: Human-subject material: IRB/ethics approval, consent scope, and (where applicable) HIPAA/GDPR constraints; store only pseudonymized identifiers in the inventory app and keep the key elsewhere
MIABIS explicitly covers only human-origin samples and the current status of stored samples - a non-human sample type needs its own vocabulary
Restrictions on sample use must be machine-readable so sharing can be blocked

fields: item name, vendor, catalog no., pack/case size, unit of issue
location (stockroom shelf, bay) + optional per-bench par locations
current quantity (packs or units), min/reorder point, max/par level
lead time (days), average weekly usage, preferred vendor + alternates
price per pack and price per unit (for real cost reporting)
sterile/RNase-free/certification flags, lot (only where it matters, e.g. filter plates)
workflows: Two-bin / kanban for fast-moving low-cost items: scan the empty-bin card to raise a request, no counting required
Min/max for higher-value or longer-lead-time items, with reorder point sized from lead-time demand plus observed variability
Barcode-scan-to-decrement at the point of use; cycle counting of a subset weekly rather than a full annual count
Auto-aggregate several small requests into one weekly bulk order per vendor to cut shipping and handling
enrichment_sources: Quartzy GET /inventory-items and /types for the existing catalog; vendor catalogs for pack sizes and prices
compliance_notes: None, but this is where adoption is won or lost: if logging a box of tips takes more than one scan, people will stop

fields: asset tag / internal ID, make, model, serial number
location (room, bench), responsible person, shared vs personal
purchase date, PO/grant, cost, warranty end, service contract + vendor contact
calibration: last date, interval, next due, certificate attachment
preventive maintenance: last date, interval, next due, checklist/SOP
service and repair history (date, vendor, fault, cost, downtime hours)
status (operational | maintenance | out of service | retired)
training/authorization required + list of trained users
booking rules (max duration, approval required, charge code)
consumables and spare parts linked to this instrument (lamps, columns, filters, O-rings)
usage log (who, when, duration, samples) for cost recovery and utilization reporting
workflows: Booking calendar that prevents double-booking and blocks selection while calibration has lapsed or PM is overdue until an admin clears the flag
Maintenance and service visits occupy the calendar the same way user bookings do, so downtime is visible before people plan around it
QR code on the instrument -> scan to see SOP, book it, log an issue, or view fault history
Automated alerts for upcoming maintenance, overdue calibration, warranty expiry and contract renewal
Utilization report per instrument to justify a replacement or a second unit
enrichment_sources: None external; vendor manuals/SOPs attached as files
compliance_notes: Calibration/PM records are the audit evidence if a result is ever questioned; keep certificates attached, not just dates
Training-and-authorization records double as the safety record for hazardous equipment (centrifuges, lasers, autoclaves, LN2 handling)

features.name: Duplicate-order interception at request time
features.description: When someone starts a purchase request, match on vendor + catalog number, CAS, Cellosaurus accession, antibody RRID, Addgene ID and fuzzy name, then show three things before they can submit: (1) what is already physically in the lab and where, (2) open requests/orders for the same item and their Quartzy status, (3) who owns them. Offer 'request an aliquot from X' or 'add my need to the existing order' as first-class alternatives to 'order new'.
features.why_it_matters: This is the PI's stated problem. Two people ordering the same antibody or cell line in the same week is detectable deterministically on identifier match, and the Quartzy order_request status enum (CREATED, CANCELLED, APPROVED, ORDERED, BACKORDERED, RECEIVED) tells you precisely whether an existing order can still be amended.

features.name: Identifier-first intake with public-API autofill
features.description: One box: paste or scan a CAS number, catalog number, RRID, Addgene ID, CVCL accession or URL, and the app resolves it against PubChem, the Antibody Registry, Addgene, Cellosaurus or hPSCreg and prefills the type-specific form. Keep the resolved identifiers as first-class indexed columns, not notes.
features.why_it_matters: Data entry is the whole adoption battle. Prefilled records are both faster and more searchable, and canonical identifiers are what make duplicate detection and reporting work at all.

features.name: Misidentified-line and problematic-line warning
features.description: On cell line creation and on a monthly re-check, test the line against Cellosaurus `problematic`/`caution`/`comment` fields and the ICLAC Register of Misidentified Cell Lines (v14, 608 lines, 560 with no known authentic stock). Show a persistent banner on the line, every bank derived from it and every experiment linked to it, naming the contaminant (e.g. HeLa, which is the contaminant in 145 register entries).
features.why_it_matters: A lab of 30 people will have at least one line on the register. Catching it before a paper is far cheaper than after, and NIH NOT-OD-15-103 already asks for an authentication plan.

features.name: Mycoplasma and STR test scheduling with hard gates
features.description: Per-line testing cadence (default: mycoplasma on arrival and then monthly or at least quarterly; STR on receipt, before banking, and before publication). Overdue tests put the line in a visible 'unverified' state; optionally block checkout of shared WCB vials or block adding the line to a manuscript export until cleared.
features.why_it_matters: Testing cadence is advisory everywhere, so it is skipped. Attaching it to the object people already touch (the vial) is the only way it happens. Quarantine of new arrivals until bacteria/fungi/mycoplasma-negative is standard banking practice.

features.name: STR profile store with one-click CLASTR match
features.description: Store per-marker alleles (Amelogenin, CSF1PO, D5S818, D7S820, D13S317, D16S539, FGA, TH01, TPOX, vWA and extended loci) and POST them to https://www.cellosaurus.org/str-search/api/query with algorithm=1 (Tanabe), scoringMode=1, minMarkers=8, scoreFilter=80. Store the top matches and scores on the line, and raise an alert when the best match is not the claimed identity.
features.why_it_matters: Turns a PDF from the core facility into a machine-checkable identity assertion. ANSI/ATCC ASN-0002-2022 uses 8 core loci + amelogenin with >=80% indicating a related sample and <50% unrelated.

features.name: Passage and population-doubling ledger with per-line ceilings
features.description: Thaw creates a culture at vial_passage + 1; each subculture records split ratio and date and auto-computes population doublings (1:2 = 1 PD, 1:4 = 2 PD) and cumulative PDL. Passage increments on reseeding, not on freezing. Warn at a per-line configurable ceiling and prompt 'discard and thaw a fresh WCB vial'.
features.why_it_matters: Passage number alone is nearly meaningless across people (a 1:4 and a 1:10 split both read as 'passage 11'), which is exactly why drift goes unnoticed in a 30-person lab. There is no universal cap, so the ceiling must be per-line and lab-set.

features.name: Tiered cell-bank manager (token / master / working)
features.description: Model banks as first-class objects: token stock (3-5 ampoules), Master Cell Bank (10-20), Working Cell Bank (20-200), each with freeze date, passage/PDL at freeze, QC results on 5-10% of vials, and an MCB-vs-WCB identity confirmation. Low-vial triggers prompt 'expand a new WCB from the MCB'.
features.why_it_matters: Personal freezer stashes exist partly because there is no trustworthy shared bank. A visible WCB with a vial count and a named owner is the thing that replaces them.

features.name: LN2 and freezer position map with scan-to-withdraw
features.description: Hierarchical locations (facility -> tank/freezer -> rack -> box/cane -> position) with a visual grid box map, every vial carrying full location data, and a full audit trail of every move. Withdrawal is a barcode scan that decrements the vial count, creates a culture record and logs who took it.
features.why_it_matters: 'It should be in the -80 somewhere' is the second-biggest waste after duplicate orders. ISBER's LN2 guidance requires unique IDs per freezer/tank/rack plus a position convention and a move audit trail; ASTM E1565 says the same in standard form.

features.name: Phone-first barcode/QR scanning (PWA, gloves-on)
features.description: A mobile web app with camera scanning of 1D and 2D DataMatrix codes, large tap targets, and three one-tap actions: 'I used some', 'I took the last one', 'where is it?'. Works for cryovial bottom DataMatrix codes, chemical container labels and equipment QR codes.
features.why_it_matters: Bench scientists with gloves on will not open a laptop. Every feature that needs a desktop is a feature that silently does not get used.

features.name: Cryo-rated label printing templates
features.description: Built-in label templates per item type that print to a thermal-transfer printer with cryo label stock rated to -196 C: strain ID on the lid and plasmid + resistance on the side for glycerol stocks; line name, passage, date and 2D code for cryovials; CAS, GHS pictograms and open-date for chemicals.
features.why_it_matters: Barcodes that fall off or smear in LN2 destroy the inventory's credibility within a month. Paper labels detach; cryo labels and burned-in thermal transfer survive.

features.name: Lot and aliquot tracking with freeze-thaw counters
features.description: Separate the catalog item (vendor + catalog no.) from the physical lot/container, and from aliquots made from it. Each aliquot carries a freeze_thaw_count incremented by checkout. Notify previous users when a new lot of an antibody, serum or enzyme arrives, and mark it 'needs re-validation'.
features.why_it_matters: Lot-to-lot variation is the main hidden cause of 'the experiment stopped working'. The Antibody Registry explicitly refuses to issue lot-level identifiers and tells researchers to report lots themselves, so the lab app is the only place this can live.

features.name: Expiry, date-opened and stability-after-opening dashboard
features.description: Track received, opened and expiry dates per container plus a type-specific 'stable for N days/months after opening' rule. A 30-day expiry dashboard per person and per room, with 'use me first' suggestions and an end-of-grant disposal list.
features.why_it_matters: Expiring-on-the-shelf reagents are a direct, quantifiable budget line the PI will see, and the same date fields drive the safety timers below.

features.name: Peroxide-former and time-sensitive chemical timers
features.description: Classify peroxide formers A/B/C at intake and auto-schedule test-or-discard tasks: Class A about 3 months after opening, Class B about 6-12 months, unopened containers at 12 months from receipt or the manufacturer expiry (whichever first). Record each peroxide test result and allow an institution-configurable interval.
features.why_it_matters: This is a genuine explosion hazard whose only control is a date on a bottle, and the receipt/open dates needed for it are already being captured for cost reasons.
seen_in: University EHS peroxide-former programs (Iowa, LSU, Illinois State, Cornell, Kentucky)

features.name: GHS hazard autofill and SDS link store
features.description: At intake, resolve CAS -> PubChem CID (/rest/pug/compound/xref/RN/{CAS}/cids/JSON) and pull GHS pictograms, signal word, H- and P-statements from PUG View (?heading=GHS+Classification), plus the LCSS link. Cache locally, store the SDS URL and version date, and render pictograms in list views and on printed labels.
features.why_it_matters: Nobody hand-enters hazard data. Automatic hazard metadata makes the inventory also serve EHS, which is how the app survives a change of lab manager. Respect PubChem's limit of 5 requests/second and 30 s per request.

features.name: Storage-compatibility check on put-away
features.description: Assign each chemical a storage group (acids, inorganic bases, flammables, oxidizers/peroxides, water-reactives, pyrophorics, highly acutely toxic/reproductive toxins) and warn when a container is filed into a location holding an incompatible group - oxidizer with flammable, acid with base, acid near cyanides, water-reactive near a sink.
features.why_it_matters: Segregation errors are the most common lab chemical finding in EHS inspections, and the app already knows both the hazard class and the exact shelf.
seen_in: Georgia Tech / Kentucky / Cornell EHS schemes

features.name: EHS and fire-code inventory export
features.description: One-click export of quantities by room and control area, grouped by hazard class, in the format campus EHS asks for, with a change log since the last submission. Include an EPCRA Tier II style threshold check (10,000 lb for SDS chemicals; 500 lb or the TPQ, whichever is lower, for Extremely Hazardous Substances) and flag anything approaching fire-code Maximum Allowable Quantities per control area.
features.why_it_matters: The annual EHS chemical inventory is currently a painful manual spreadsheet exercise; making it a by-product gives the lab manager a concrete reason to keep the data clean all year.

features.name: Regulated-material flag with escalation, not local rules
features.description: A flag set per item for 'institutionally regulated' categories (DEA-scheduled substances, select biological agents/toxins, export-controlled, radioactive) which hides normal self-service workflows and instead routes the user to the named institutional officer plus the required program record. The app records that an item is in scope and who is responsible; it does not encode the regulatory rules.
features.why_it_matters: Getting these categories wrong is a serious institutional problem, and the rules change. A flag-and-escalate design is both safer and far less work than trying to implement the regulations.

features.name: Controlled-substance perpetual log and biennial count report
features.description: For DEA-registered items, a tamper-evident receipt-to-disposal log (date, user, amount used, amount remaining, witness), Schedule I-II records kept separate from III-V, a biennial physical-inventory report generator, and disposal records naming the reverse distributor. Immutable append-only entries with signatures.
features.why_it_matters: Current practice is paper logs in a drawer that fail audits. Only build this if the lab actually holds scheduled substances, and build it with the institutional controlled-substance program, referencing 21 CFR 1301/1304.
seen_in: UF, UCLA, UMich, WCU controlled-substance programs

features.name: Biosafety and IBC protocol linkage
features.description: Attach BSL and the IBC/IRB protocol number to cell lines, viral vectors, strains and human samples. Show the required containment on the item card and on the printed label, and warn when a human or primate line is registered without a BSL-2 designation or a protocol number.
features.why_it_matters: Human and other primate cell lines are handled at BSL-2 under BMBL guidance, and OSHA's interpretation brings human cell lines into the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard unless characterized free of bloodborne pathogens. Most IBCs require a registered protocol and annual training records.
seen_in: URI / LSU / UCLA / UCI / UT Austin biosafety manuals

features.name: MTA, license and onward-transfer gate
features.description: Store incoming MTA/UBMTA Implementing Letter or Simple Letter Agreement per material, with structured flags for academic-only, no-redistribution, publication-notice-required and derivative ownership. Outgoing share requests check the flags and route to the tech-transfer office when needed.
features.why_it_matters: Patient-derived lines, Addgene deposits and collaborator strains come with real restrictions that are currently remembered by one person. Encoding them prevents an accidental breach and speeds legitimate sharing.

features.name: Plasmid sequence files, maps and verification status
features.description: Attach GenBank (.gb) and SnapGene (.dna) files, render a map, parse features and resistance markers from the file, and require an attached sequencing/alignment result before a construct can be marked 'sequence verified'. Link each plasmid to the strains and glycerol stocks that carry it.
features.why_it_matters: Re-cloning something a labmate already made and verified is the plasmid equivalent of a duplicate order, and it costs weeks rather than dollars.

features.name: Strain lineage and genotype graph
features.description: Enforce parental_strain and plasmid links at freeze-down, then render a lineage tree: 'everything derived from BL21(DE3)', 'every strain carrying pLAB-0123'. Require a duplicate backup tube in a second freezer and record both positions.
features.why_it_matters: Strain collections decay into unreadable tube labels within two generations of students. The lineage link is what keeps a strain usable after its creator leaves - the single biggest institutional-memory loss in an academic lab.

features.name: Oligo and primer registry with sequence search and resuspension calculator
features.description: Search primers by exact sequence and reverse complement as well as by name and target gene. On receipt, compute resuspension volume (uL for 100 uM = nmol x 10, using delivered nmol, not ordered scale) and write buffer, concentration and date into the record. Default buffer guidance: IDTE pH 7.5/8.0 or nuclease-free water, not DEPC-treated or deionized water.
features.why_it_matters: Oligos are cheap individually and re-ordered constantly; sequence search is the only dedup that works because names are personal. Validated primer pairs are also reusable lab IP.

features.name: Per-application antibody dilution table
features.description: On each antibody, a crowd-edited table of application (WB, IF, IHC-P, FC, IP, ChIP), dilution or concentration, diluent/blocking buffer, sample type, who tried it, date, and worked/failed with an image link. Separate 'vendor-claimed' from 'validated in this lab'.
features.why_it_matters: This is the single most valuable piece of tribal knowledge in a wet lab and it currently lives in notebooks. It also gives people a selfish reason to open the app, which is how the inventory data stays current.

features.name: Methods-section and RRID export
features.description: Select the materials used in a figure or paper and export a formatted methods paragraph with full provenance: cell line name + RRID:CVCL_xxxx + source catalog no. + passage range + last STR/mycoplasma dates; antibody vendor + cat# + lot + clone + host + RRID:AB_xxxxxxx + dilution; plasmid + Addgene ID; chemical + CAS + vendor + lot.
features.why_it_matters: Converts compliance burden into a visible personal benefit at exactly the moment people care (submission), and satisfies journal reporting checklists and the NIH authentication attachment with no extra bookkeeping.

features.name: Personal-stash amnesty and claim-a-vial
features.description: A deliberately low-friction bulk-import path for personal inventories (photo of a freezer box, CSV paste, or scan-a-box mode), with the owner keeping 'custodian' status and a 'shareable / ask me first / mine' setting per item. Items visible to all; a request button notifies the owner.
features.why_it_matters: Personal inventories exist because sharing felt costly and risky, not out of malice. Letting people keep custody while making stock visible removes the incentive to hide, and visibility - not confiscation - is what stops duplicate orders.

features.name: Low-stock and reorder-point suggestions from real usage
features.description: Compute average consumption from checkout events, then suggest reorder points as lead-time demand plus a safety buffer, with min/max for high-value or long-lead items and a simple two-bin/kanban card for cheap fast-movers. Auto-batch pending requests per vendor into a weekly order.
features.why_it_matters: Replaces panic ordering (which causes both duplicates and rush shipping) with a predictable weekly cycle, and batching per vendor cuts shipping and handling.

features.name: Quartzy two-way sync
features.description: Poll or webhook Quartzy to mirror inventory items (name, vendor, catalog_number, cas_number, lot_number, expiration_date, price, unit_size, quantity, location/sublocation pathNames, instances) and order requests (status, vendor_name, catalog_number, quantity, unit_price, total_price, requested_by, tracking_number, purchase_order_number, is_urgent). Write back quantity updates via PUT /inventory-items/{itemId}/instances/{itemInstanceId}.
features.why_it_matters: Nobody will abandon the purchasing system the institution pays for. Quartzy's REST API (base https://api.quartzy.com, Access-Token header, page parameter, webhooks with signing keys) makes 'is it already on order?' answerable without changing anyone's purchasing habits - the lowest-risk path to making the new app immediately useful.

features.name: Spend and waste reporting for the PI
features.description: Dashboards for spend by category, by person, by grant code (Quartzy exposes spend_tracking_code), avoided duplicate orders (count and dollar value of intercepted requests), expired-unused value, and items with the highest reorder frequency. Monthly digest email to the PI.
features.why_it_matters: The project was commissioned because of cost. A number the PI can quote in a lab meeting - 'we intercepted 14 duplicate requests worth $9,400 this quarter' - is what keeps the app funded and mandated.

features.name: Equipment maintenance, calibration and booking with hard blocks
features.description: Asset records (make, model, serial, location, warranty, service contract), calibration and PM intervals with next-due dates, service/fault history, a booking calendar that prevents double-booking, and automatic blocking of bookings while calibration is lapsed or PM is overdue until an admin clears it. Maintenance windows occupy the calendar like bookings do.
features.why_it_matters: Shared instruments are the other contested resource in a 30-person lab, and the same scan-a-QR-code habit that drives inventory also drives equipment logs and fault reporting.

features.name: Notification routing people actually tolerate
features.description: Per-user digests rather than per-event emails, with routing rules: expiry and test-due to the item owner, duplicate-order interception to the requester and lab manager, safety timers to the safety officer, and a weekly lab-wide 'arriving / expiring / low stock' summary. Slack/Teams and email channels.
features.why_it_matters: Reminder fatigue kills these systems faster than missing features; a daily per-item email will get the whole app filtered to trash in week two.

features.name: Offline-tolerant bench mode
features.description: Queue scans and quantity decrements locally when there is no signal (cold rooms, basements, LN2 facilities) and sync when connectivity returns, with conflict resolution on quantity fields.
features.why_it_matters: The places where inventory changes - cold rooms, tissue-culture suites, LN2 facilities - are exactly the places with no wifi. A spinner at the freezer door is how people learn to stop logging.

features.name: Audit trail and leaver handover
features.description: Append-only history on every record (who changed what, when, old and new value), plus a 'person is leaving' report listing everything they own, with bulk reassignment of custody and an orphaned-item queue.
features.why_it_matters: Student and postdoc turnover is the main way a lab loses track of material. Handover as a first-class workflow is what prevents the next generation of mystery boxes, and the audit trail is what makes a shared inventory trustworthy enough that people stop keeping private copies.

features.name: Nightly enrichment reconciliation
features.description: A scheduled job that re-queries public sources for items already in the inventory: new Cellosaurus release (via /release-info) changing a problematic flag, an antibody newly marked discontinued, a new ICLAC register version, a changed GHS classification, an Addgene bulk dataset refresh (daily, versioned majorVersion.minorVersion). Surface deltas as a review queue, never silent overwrites.
features.why_it_matters: Reference data about a material changes after you buy it - a line becomes known-misidentified, an antibody is discontinued before you need more. A review queue keeps curation honest while staying inside published rate limits.

features.name: AI assist for messy intake
features.description: Photo of a bottle label, a packing slip or a freezer box lid -> extract vendor, catalog number, lot, CAS, expiry and position grid, then present them as a pre-filled form for human confirmation. Natural-language search ('secondary anti-rabbit HRP that someone has validated for WB').
features.why_it_matters: The one-time migration of ~30 personal inventories is the biggest single barrier to launch, and most of that data exists only as label photos and handwritten box maps.

key_insights: The domain is not one inventory - it is roughly 14 schemas with one shared skeleton (identity, location, amount, owner, lot, dates, status) plus a type-specific payload. Build a polymorphic core with per-type field definitions (JSONB or an EAV-lite table with typed field specs) rather than one wide table or 14 unrelated models.

Identity keys differ fundamentally by type, and that determines whether duplicate detection works: antibodies are identified by vendor + catalog number (the Antibody Registry's own primary key), chemicals by CAS/PubChem CID, cell lines by Cellosaurus CVCL accession plus source collection catalog number, plasmids by Addgene ID, oligos only by sequence. Dedup must be per-type, not one fuzzy name match.

Lot is the unit that breaks experiments, and no public registry will track it. The Antibody Registry explicitly declined to issue lot-level identifiers because of cost, and tells researchers to report lots in methods instead - so catalog item -> lot -> aliquot must be three distinct levels in the data model from day one.

Passage number is not comparable between people: a 1:4 and a 1:10 split of the same culture both produce 'passage 11'. Recording split ratio and deriving cumulative population doublings is the only way passage data from 30 different hands means anything. Also: passage increments on reseeding, not on freezing, and thaw+reseed counts as one passage.

There is no universal passage cap or mycoplasma testing interval in any authoritative source - ATCC says passage effects are line-specific and a window must be established per line, and testing recommendations range from monthly (LCSB) to every 3-6 months (vendor minimums). So these must be per-item configurable policies with lab-set defaults, never hard-coded constants.

The best enrichment APIs are free and unauthenticated: Cellosaurus (CC BY 4.0), CLASTR, PubChem PUG-REST/PUG View (<=5 req/s), the Antibody Registry API, UniProt, NCBI E-utilities (3 req/s, 10 with a key). Only Addgene needs an approval process (per-scope data access license, ~5 business days, token valid 1 year) and CAS Common Chemistry needs a requested key with CC BY-NC terms. A one-person build can realistically wire all of them.

Quartzy already models the exact objects needed for duplicate prevention and exposes them over REST: /inventory-items (with cas_number, lot_number, expiration_date, location.pathNames, instances) and /order-requests with a 6-state status enum (CREATED, CANCELLED, APPROVED, ORDERED, BACKORDERED, RECEIVED), plus webhooks with signing keys. The app does not need to replace purchasing - it needs to read the pipeline and interject at request time.

Compliance work the lab already owes is the app's second value proposition and its survival strategy: the NIH authentication attachment (NOT-OD-15-103), BSL-2/IBC registration for human cell lines (OSHA BBP interpretation + BMBL), peroxide-former test timers, the annual campus EHS chemical inventory, MTA onward-transfer limits. These are things a spreadsheet cannot do, which is what justifies the app over 'just use a shared sheet'.

Personal inventories are a rational response to bad shared systems, not a discipline problem. The design answer is custodianship (visible to all, owned by one, with an 'ask me' request button) rather than confiscation - visibility alone eliminates the duplicate orders without requiring anyone to hand over their stock.

Physical-layer details decide whether the system survives: cryo labels must be rated to about -196 C because paper detaches, vials belong in the LN2 vapour phase, 2D DataMatrix beats 1D for small vials, and ISBER/ASTM E1565 both require a unique code for every freezer, rack, box and position plus an audit trail on every move. Software that ignores the label stock will have unreadable barcodes within one freezer season.

Enrichment data drifts after purchase: a cell line can be added to the ICLAC register (v14, 15 Feb 2026, 608 lines), an antibody can be discontinued (about 303k such records in the registry), a GHS classification can change. Treat public data as a cached, versioned snapshot with a scheduled re-check and a human review queue, not as a one-time copy.

For biospecimens, do not invent a schema: MIABIS Core 3.0 (32 attributes) plus its individual-level extension - whose sample attributes were drawn from ISBER's SPREC - already defines sample type, anatomical source, storage temperature, creation date, use restrictions and the event model. Adopting it also makes any future biobank collaboration far easier.
recommendations: Phase 1 should be only: identifier-first intake with public-API autofill, hierarchical locations with a box map, phone barcode scanning, lot/aliquot/expiry tracking, and the Quartzy duplicate-order interceptor. That set alone addresses the PI's stated problem; everything else is sequencing.

Ship the duplicate-order check as a read-only overlay on the existing Quartzy workflow first (a 'check before you request' screen plus a Slack bot), so adoption needs no behavior change and the first measurable win arrives in weeks, not months.

Make the first killer feature a selfish one: the per-application antibody dilution table and the primer sequence search. People will open an app that saves them a failed Western; the inventory data then stays current as a side effect of them using it.

Model cell lines, banks, vials and cultures as four separate entities (line -> bank -> vial -> culture). Collapsing bank or culture into the vial record is the mistake that makes passage history, QC provenance and withdrawal audit impossible to add later.

Store the resolved public identifiers - cellosaurus_accession, antibody RRID, pubchem_cid, addgene_id, uniprot_accession, cas_number - as indexed first-class columns with a `source`, `fetched_at` and raw-payload JSONB cache. Never overwrite a curated field with a refreshed API value; queue the delta for review.

Build one enrichment-client module per source behind a single internal interface (resolve(identifier) -> normalized record), with per-source rate limiting and on-disk caching. Respect PubChem's 5 req/s and 30 s limits and NCBI's 3 req/s (10 with a registered API key plus tool and email values).

Apply for the Addgene Developers Portal token now - it needs an approved access request with a per-scope data access license and takes about five business days, the token expires annually, and antibodies, pooled libraries, kits and bacterial strains are announced for the Catalog API in late 2026.

Make all cadences data, not code: mycoplasma interval, STR interval, passage/PDL ceiling, peroxide-former class intervals, calibration intervals. Authoritative guidance genuinely varies by institution and by cell line, so hard-coded numbers will be wrong and will be used as a reason to distrust the app.

Flag-and-escalate for regulated categories (DEA-scheduled substances, select agents/toxins, export-controlled, radioactive): mark the item as in-scope, name the responsible institutional officer, and link out to the institutional program. Do not attempt to implement the regulations in the app, and involve the biosafety officer and EHS before storing any such records.

Buy the label stock and the thermal-transfer printer before writing the labelling code, and test a printed label in LN2 and in a -80 freezer for a week. Choose 2D DataMatrix for cryovials and validate that a phone camera can read it at the size your vials allow.

Budget real effort for migration: a bulk-import path (CSV paste, photo-of-box-lid OCR, scan-a-box mode) plus a one-day 'amnesty' event where people register their personal stashes and keep custody. Treat it as an explicit project phase with the lab manager, not an afterthought.

Run the duplicate-prevention metric from day one - count and dollar-value of intercepted requests, expired-unused value, items reordered most often - and put it in a monthly digest to the PI. It is both the project's justification and the evidence needed to make use mandatory.

Define ownership and succession before launch: a named data steward (likely the lab manager, not the bioinformatician), a documented leaver-handover workflow, and a plain-text/CSV export of everything. A one-maintainer app in a 30-person wet lab must survive the maintainer's thesis defense.
pitfalls: Hard-coding guidance numbers as if they were standards. There is no authoritative universal passage cap, mycoplasma interval, or peroxide-former timer - ATCC says passage effects are line-specific, testing recommendations range from monthly to every 3-6 months, and peroxide-former intervals differ between universities. Wrong constants become a credibility problem.

Treating the catalog item as the physical thing. Without catalog item -> lot -> aliquot separation you cannot track freeze-thaw counts, cannot alert on a lot change, cannot record per-lot QC, and cannot export a usable methods section. Retrofitting this split later means migrating every record.
Trusting that passage numbers from different people are comparable, or incrementing passage on freezing. Both silently corrupt the one field cell biologists care most about.

Copying public reference data once and treating it as static. ICLAC releases new register versions (v13 April 2024 with 593 lines; v14 February 2026 with 608), Cellosaurus has releases, antibodies get discontinued, GHS classifications change. Snapshot with provenance and re-check on a schedule.

Ignoring data licenses. Cellosaurus is CC BY 4.0, the ICLAC register is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (attribution required, no modification of entries, download from ICLAC to get the current version), CAS Common Chemistry non-commercial use is CC BY-NC 4.0 with a separate commercial license, Addgene requires accepting a data access license per API scope. Scraping Sigma-Aldrich or Thermo catalogs instead of using their APIs risks both terms violations and silent breakage.

Exceeding published rate limits during a bulk backfill. PubChem asks for no more than 5 requests/second with a 30 s per-request limit and can temporarily block an IP; NCBI E-utilities caps at 3 requests/second without a key. A naive migration script over 3,000 chemicals will get the lab's IP throttled.

Designing for the desktop. Gloves, cold rooms with no wifi, and 30 seconds of patience are the real constraints. Any workflow that needs more than one scan plus one tap will be abandoned, and an abandoned shared inventory recreates the personal-stash problem it was built to solve.
Notification spam. Per-event emails for every expiry and test-due will train the lab to filter the app's mail, after which every safety reminder it sends is also invisible.

Using paper or non-cryo labels, or submerging vials in liquid nitrogen. Labels detach and codes become unreadable, and liquid-phase storage risks vial failure and cross-contamination - the inventory then silently diverges from the freezer.
Storing identifiable donor data in the inventory app. Keep pseudonymized IDs, structured consent flags and a pointer to the system of record; the key belongs elsewhere, under IRB-approved control.
Mandating the system before it is faster than the status quo. If the first encounter is a 20-field form, people will do what they do now and the PI will conclude the problem is cultural.

Building the controlled-substance and EHS modules early. They are the highest-compliance, lowest-adoption parts of the app and depend on institutional processes you do not control - they should follow a working core, and be designed with EHS and the biosafety officer rather than for them.
open_questions: Does the lab's Quartzy plan include API access, and can the user get an AccessToken plus webhook configuration rights for the lab's organization? Quartzy's documented rate limits are absent, so throughput for a sync job needs to be measured or confirmed with support.

Does the institution already run a central chemical inventory system (MyChem, ChemTracker/Stanford-derived, EHSA, BioRAFT)? If so, the chemical module may need to feed that system rather than duplicate it, and the required export format should be obtained from EHS before designing the chemical schema.

Which item types actually exist in meaningful numbers in this lab? A 30-person wet lab is unlikely to need controlled substances, biospecimens and pooled CRISPR libraries all at once, and each type carries real schema and workflow cost.

Does the lab hold any DEA-scheduled substances, select agents or toxins, or export-controlled material? If yes, the biosafety officer and institutional controlled-substance program must be involved before any such record is designed or stored.

How many LN2 tanks, -80 freezers and -20 freezers exist, and what is the physical rack/box geometry? The location hierarchy and box-map UI depend on real tank layouts, and existing cane-vs-box storage determines whether position coordinates are 2D grids or linear cane positions.

What does the current personal-inventory data look like - spreadsheets, notebook pages, photos, or nothing? This determines whether migration is a CSV importer, an OCR pipeline, or a scan-a-box data-entry sprint.

Is there an existing ELN (Benchling, LabArchives, eLabFTW, SciNote)? If so, the inventory should link to experiments there rather than build its own experiment layer, and the ELN's inventory module should be evaluated first to avoid building a duplicate.

Can the lab buy a thermal-transfer label printer and cryo-rated label stock, and is there an existing barcode convention on vials that must be preserved? Retrofitting barcodes onto tens of thousands of existing vials may be infeasible, which argues for barcoding at next-touch instead of a full relabelling campaign.

Who will be the data steward when the user graduates or moves on, and will the PI mandate use? Without a named non-bioinformatician owner and an explicit mandate, the most likely failure mode is a technically good app that half the lab ignores.

Does the Antibody Registry's /api endpoint have official documentation and stated terms? The endpoint paths currently come from a third-party wrapper, so they should be confirmed with the registry (rii-help@scicrunch.org) before being depended on in production.

What is the real annual cost of the problem? A baseline from Quartzy order history (duplicate catalog numbers ordered within N days by different people, plus expired-unused spend) would both size the project and provide the before/after number the PI wants.

tech_components.need: Resolve and cache public identifier metadata (Cellosaurus, PubChem, Antibody Registry, Addgene, UniProt, NCBI) with per-source rate limits
tech_components.recommended: One async client per source behind a common resolve(identifier) interface, using httpx.AsyncClient + tenacity for retries/backoff, a token-bucket limiter per source, and a Postgres JSONB cache table (source, external_id, payload, fetched_at, etag)
tech_components.rationale: Each source has different auth, limits and licensing (PubChem <=5 req/s and 30 s/request; NCBI 3 req/s or 10 with a key; Addgene token-gated with annual expiry; CAS Common Chemistry keyed and CC BY-NC). A single interface keeps the per-type intake code clean and makes the nightly reconciliation job reuse the same code path as interactive lookup.
gotchas: PubChem sits behind a browser-verification interstitial for HTML doc pages but the /rest/ endpoints are fine - do not scrape the docs
GHS lives in PUG View (/rest/pug_view/data/compound/{cid}/JSON?heading=GHS+Classification), not PUG REST properties
Cache raw payloads so a schema change upstream does not lose data already fetched

tech_components.recommended: Postgres with a shared `items` table plus a `item_type` and a validated JSONB `attributes` column, driven by per-type field definitions (name, label, datatype, unit, required, enum, enrichment source); Pydantic models generated from those definitions for validation
tech_components.rationale: Field sets genuinely differ per material type and will keep changing as the lab adopts the app; JSONB with GIN indexes gives per-type flexibility while keeping the shared skeleton (location, amount, owner, lot, dates) relational and queryable for duplicate detection and reporting.
alternatives: 14 concrete tables with a shared base via Django multi-table inheritance
gotchas: Keep identifiers (cas_number, cellosaurus_accession, rrid, addgene_id) as real indexed columns, not inside JSONB, or dedup queries will be slow and fragile
Validate enums server-side; a free-text unit field will quietly destroy any quantity arithmetic

tech_components.need: Phone barcode/QR scanning in a browser
tech_components.recommended: A PWA front end using the browser camera with zxing-cpp (WASM) or html5-qrcode for 1D plus 2D DataMatrix decoding; service worker + IndexedDB queue for offline scan buffering
tech_components.rationale: No app-store distribution, works on both iOS and Android, and installable to the home screen - essential for a one-maintainer project. Offline buffering matters because cold rooms and LN2 facilities usually have no signal.
alternatives: Native app (too much maintenance for one person)
dedicated USB/Bluetooth 2D scanner at fixed stations
gotchas: DataMatrix on cryovial bottoms is small; test real vials under real lighting before committing to phone-only scanning
iOS Safari camera APIs require HTTPS and explicit user gesture
Design idempotent scan events so a replayed offline queue cannot double-decrement a quantity

tech_components.recommended: Thermal-transfer printer (Zebra or Brady class) with cryo-rated label stock rated to about -196 C; generate labels server-side as ZPL or as PDF via reportlab, and render 2D DataMatrix with treepoem (Ghostscript/BWIPP) or python-barcode for 1D
tech_components.rationale: Thermal transfer burns the image in so it survives abrasion and LN2, which direct-thermal and office laser labels do not. Server-side generation keeps templates versioned with the app rather than in one person's label software.
alternatives: DYMO/Brother label makers for non-cryo items
pre-barcoded 2D DataMatrix cryovials (vendor-assigned unique codes, no printing needed)
gotchas: Paper labels detach at -80/-196 C; budget for proper label stock
Pre-barcoded vials remove printing entirely but lock you to a vial vendor and need a bulk code-import path
treepoem needs Ghostscript installed - a real deployment dependency

tech_components.need: Scheduled reminders, test-due timers and nightly enrichment reconciliation
tech_components.recommended: Celery with Celery Beat (Redis broker) for a Django app, or APScheduler/arq for a FastAPI app; model due dates as stored fields plus a daily job that materializes tasks, rather than computing them at read time
tech_components.rationale: Mycoplasma/STR due dates, peroxide-former timers, calibration due dates and expiry digests are all the same pattern. Storing materialized due dates makes them queryable, dashboard-able and testable, and keeps notification batching (digests, not per-event mail) straightforward.
gotchas: Batch notifications into digests from the start; per-event email will get the app filtered
Make every interval a per-item configurable policy with a lab default, since the underlying guidance varies by institution and by cell line

tech_components.need: Sequence file handling for plasmids, oligos and guides
tech_components.recommended: Biopython (SeqIO) to parse and write GenBank/FASTA, extract features and resistance markers, and compute Tm/GC/MW; store original .gb and SnapGene .dna files as opaque attachments with checksums; render maps client-side with a JS plasmid viewer (e.g. seqviz)
tech_components.rationale: Parsing GenBank features lets the app prefill resistance marker, insert and tags from an uploaded map, and sequence-level storage is what makes exact-match and reverse-complement primer search possible - the only dedup that works for oligos.
gotchas: SnapGene .dna is proprietary - keep the original file and treat any parse as best-effort
Index primer sequences both as given and reverse-complemented so search finds a pair someone entered in the other orientation

tech_components.need: Deployment a single bioinformatician can maintain for years
tech_components.recommended: Django + Django REST Framework + Postgres + Redis, HTMX or a small React front end, all in Docker Compose on an institutional VM or managed host, with nightly pg_dump plus an always-available CSV/Excel export of every table
tech_components.rationale: Django gives the admin interface, auth, migrations and permissions almost free, which is exactly the leverage a one-person project needs for a 30-user internal app. The plain-text export is the honest insurance policy: if maintenance lapses, the lab still has its data.
alternatives: FastAPI + SQLModel (more control, more hand-written admin)
adopting eLabFTW or SENAITE and extending it
gotchas: Use institutional SSO (SAML/OIDC) rather than local passwords so leaver offboarding is automatic
Check whether institutional policy requires the app and any human-subject-derived data to live on managed infrastructure before choosing a host
Resist adding an ELN - if the lab has Benchling or LabArchives, link to it instead

products.name: Quartzy
products.license_or_pricing: Free tier plus paid plans; API access via an AccessToken in the Access-Token header (OAuth2 also listed)
strengths: Already in use for purchasing, so no behavior change is needed
REST API exposes both /inventory-items and /order-requests with a clear status enum (CREATED, CANCELLED, APPROVED, ORDERED, BACKORDERED, RECEIVED)
Inventory item fields already include cas_number, lot_number, expiration_date, location/sublocation pathNames and per-instance quantities
Webhooks with signing keys for event-driven sync
weaknesses: No standalone locations endpoint - location exists only as nested objects on items, so a true freezer/box map cannot be modelled
No per-type schemas for cell lines, plasmids, strains or antibodies; no passage, STR, mycoplasma or RRID concepts
Rate limits undocumented; PUT /inventory-items/{id} is deprecated in favour of the instance endpoint
No public-database enrichment
standout_features: Order-request status pipeline that makes 'already on order' answerable
Spend tracking codes for grant attribution
products.fit_notes: Keep as the system of record for purchasing and read from it; the new app should add the per-type depth, location map and duplicate interception that Quartzy structurally cannot provide.
products.activity: Actively maintained developer portal with a changelog and RSS/Atom feeds

products.name: Benchling (Inventory + Registry)
strengths: Well-designed four-object location model (locations, containers, boxes, plates) with barcode prefixes per schema and metadata fields on location schemas
Box and plate schemas constrain which container types they can hold
Strong registry for DNA/protein entities, which maps cleanly onto plasmids and oligos
weaknesses: Inventory is secondary to the ELN/registry story; comparisons rate its inventory as merely 'available' rather than a strength
No native procurement or duplicate-order prevention against an external purchasing system
Cost and configuration overhead are significant for a 30-person academic lab
products.fit_notes: The locations/containers/boxes/plates hierarchy is the single best model to copy for the freezer and LN2 layer, whether or not the lab adopts Benchling.

products.name: eLabFTW
strengths: Mature open-source ELN with built-in inventory ('database' items), scheduling and authentication
Self-hostable, which suits institutional data policies
Active community and frequent releases
weaknesses: PHP/MySQL, not Python - extending it means working outside the maintainer's main language
Inventory is generic items rather than material-type-specific schemas with passage, lot or STR semantics
No procurement integration or duplicate-order detection
standout_features: Combined ELN + inventory + equipment scheduling in one self-hosted app
products.fit_notes: Worth evaluating as a base before building from scratch, especially if the lab also wants an ELN; the gap to fill would be type-specific schemas, enrichment APIs and the Quartzy duplicate check.

products.name: SENAITE (fork of Bika LIMS)
strengths: Python-based with RESTful APIs and a modular, extensible architecture
Mature sample and analysis workflow engine
weaknesses: Built on Plone, which is a steep and unusual stack for a bioinformatician who knows Django/FastAPI
Oriented toward service/analytical labs and sample throughput rather than research material inventory
Inventory of product and reference materials was historically a gap in Bika
products.fit_notes: Python, but the Plone dependency makes it a poor fit for a one-person research-lab build; study its workflow modelling rather than adopting it.

products.name: Calira (formerly ClusterMarket) / LabLynx / Labii equipment modules
strengths: Real-time booking calendars with approval workflows, role-based permissions and training-gated access
Automatic booking blocks during maintenance downtime and when calibration has lapsed or PM is overdue
Per-instrument utilization reports useful for justifying purchases
Labii tracks make/model/serial/calibration dates with automated alerts and billable usage logs
weaknesses: Feature claims come from vendor marketing, not independent verification
Separate subscription and separate login from the inventory system
Core-facility billing complexity is overkill for a single lab
standout_features: Hard block on booking an out-of-calibration instrument until an admin clears the flag
Maintenance windows occupying the booking calendar like user bookings
products.fit_notes: The calibration/PM hard-block pattern is the feature worth reimplementing; a single lab probably does not need a separate commercial booking platform.
