research.angle: dupes_adoption: the PI's core problem (duplicate orders, hidden personal inventories) and why lab inventory systems succeed or fail in academic labs
research.summary:
Duplicate orders in a 30-person wet lab come from two things: people can't see what exists, and the same item goes by many names. Quartzy, which the lab already uses, covers only a small part of this. Its duplicate-request notification fires only when the catalog number is identical, only inside the same Quartzy Lab, and only against open requests (New, Approved, Ordered or Backordered). It never checks inventory, personal stock, other vendors or other pack sizes, and a stale 'Ordered' request keeps triggering the warning forever.

Quartzy does have a usable REST API: order-requests, inventory-items with instances, and webhooks that are CloudEvents with HMAC-SHA256 signatures. So the best design is a companion app on top of Quartzy that keeps Quartzy as the place purchases are made. The app would:
- check every new request, and every request at approval, against inventory, personal shelves and open requests
- normalize vendors and catalog numbers, and group equivalent products by shared identifiers (HeLa alone has 25+ provider catalog IDs in Cellosaurus)
- create inventory automatically when an order is received
- let people update stock with one tap after a scan
- let personal stock stay owned but visible, with borrowing and lending

There are almost no independent numbers on how much labs lose to duplicate orders. The widely quoted figures (25% of time spent searching, 2-5% of inventory thrown out, 97% time savings, a '10-second rule') are vendor claims with no source. More credible evidence comes from sharing and visibility programs:
- LEAF pilot: 235 lab groups saved an average of GBP 3,700 per year each
- UCL Chemistry: up to GBP 90k per year from cataloguing and sharing chemicals in Quartzy (self-reported)
- University of Michigan Lab Swap Shop: over $1M in avoided costs in under 2 years

Anecdotes back this up: one Yale lab kept up to 20 copies of a sample where 2-3 would do, and a lab manager in a Thermo Fisher paid endorsement said 'four different people had ordered MEM'. The lab should therefore measure its own baseline from Quartzy order history.

The adoption evidence is consistent. Systems fail when:
- data entry is a separate chore
- one superuser ends up typing for everyone
- training happens once, at launch
- workarounds go untracked

They succeed when:
- receiving an order creates the inventory record
- stock is updated at the point of use
- personal stock remains owned rather than confiscated
- the PI backs explicit rules: search before ordering, give a reason to override a warning, mark items received with a location
- there is a named owner, bench champions, training in waves, weekly digests and periodic stocktakes

Limitations: Reddit (r/labrats, r/LabManagement) blocks this crawler, so I used review sites (Capterra, Software Advice/GetApp), Hacker News and lab wikis for user sentiment instead. The shared web-search budget ran out partway, so a few details are marked as unverified or inferred.

features.name: Pre-order duplicate check across inventory, personal shelves and open requests
features.description: Runs whenever someone starts a request: the in-app form, a Slack /order command or the browser extension. For requests created directly in Quartzy, it runs within about a minute of the order-request webhook. Matching works in three tiers: (1) exact normalized product key (canonical vendor + catalog_key); (2) same equivalence group (Cellosaurus CVCL_ for cell lines, RRID AB_ for antibodies, CAS for chemicals, Addgene ID for plasmids); (3) fuzzy name match restricted to the same item type (pg_trgm finds candidates, RapidFuzz scores them). It searches all inventory instances including personal 'My shelf' items, open Quartzy requests (CREATED/APPROVED/ORDERED/BACKORDERED), and items RECEIVED in the last 30 days that may not be shelved yet. The result card shows owner, location path, quantity, expiry, and request status and age. Actions: Borrow from owner / Add my quantity to the existing request / Order anyway (reason picklist: need fresh lot, contamination concern, not enough quantity, different application). Every outcome is written to a duplicate_events table with an estimated $ avoided (unit_price x qty).
features.why_it_matters: This is the PI's core problem. Quartzy's built-in check only matches an identical catalog # in the same Quartzy Lab against open requests. It never looks at inventory, personal stock, other vendors or pack sizes, which is exactly where this lab's duplicates come from.
seen_in: Quartzy duplicate request notification (catalog-#-only, same Lab, open statuses)
LabCup at Trinity College Dublin TCBE (check before buying)

features.name: Approver queue with duplicate panel and merge/decline actions
features.description: For whoever approves Quartzy requests (lab manager or PI). Each pending request shows: matching inventory, with the requester's own holdings highlighted; other open requests for the same product or equivalence group; the last 3 purchase prices and vendors; and cheaper equivalents. One-click actions: Merge into request #N (raise its quantity and cancel the duplicate), Decline and borrow from X (notifies both people), Approve. Status is pushed back with PUT /order-requests/{id} (status enum CREATED, APPROVED, ORDERED, BACKORDERED, RECEIVED, CANCELLED). The app mirrors Quartzy's 'Automatically approve requests when the total is below' threshold so cheap consumables aren't slowed down.
features.why_it_matters: Approval is the last cheap point to stop a duplicate. NMSU Chemical Engineering does this by hand: the lab manager checks whether the requester already holds the material and withholds approval until it is used up or disposed of. The app turns that search into a 5-second glance.
seen_in: Quartzy request approvals with price threshold

features.name: Product master with vendor and catalog-number normalization
features.description:
One product table that every request and inventory item links to. Fields:
- vendor_raw and vendor_canonical, using an alias table (e.g. Gibco/Invitrogen/Life Technologies/Applied Biosystems -> Thermo Fisher Scientific; Sigma-Aldrich/MilliporeSigma -> Merck)
- catalog_raw and catalog_key (uppercase, spaces/hyphens/dots stripped)
- pack_size, split off the catalog suffix when the vendor encodes size in the number (per-vendor regex; exact suffix conventions not verified here)
- product_family_id grouping pack sizes
- item_type
- external identifiers (CAS, RRID, Cellosaurus, Addgene)
- lab_standard flag
Seed it from 12-24 months of Quartzy order history (GET /order-requests) and current Quartzy inventory (GET /inventory-items). The lab manager can then merge or split clusters.
features.why_it_matters: Free-text names and formatting differences (e.g. 'anti-CD3 antibody' vs 'aCD3 Ab', '11965-092' vs '11965092') hide duplicates from both spreadsheets and exact-match checks. A single canonical product record is what makes 'who has this?' answerable. (These examples are mine, not from a source.)
seen_in: Lab Manager advice to keep a catalog of records to prevent duplicate entries
Quartzy support team offers manual 'finding equivalent matches'

features.name: Cross-vendor equivalence groups (identifier-based)
features.description:
Groups products that are the same biological or chemical thing regardless of vendor:
- cell lines by Cellosaurus accession (HeLa CVCL_0030 = ATCC CCL-2 = ECACC 93021013 = DSMZ ACC-57 = JCRB9004 = RIKEN RCB0007 = CLS 300194, plus about 20 more provider IDs)
- antibodies by RRID plus target/clone/host/conjugate
- chemicals by CAS/InChIKey
- plasmids by Addgene ID
The lab manager can also add manual 'interchangeable' links (e.g. two FBS products the lab treats as equivalent) and mark a 'lab standard'. The duplicate check and the approver panel both use these groups.
features.why_it_matters: Matching on catalog number, which is what Quartzy does, cannot see that someone ordering HeLa from ECACC is duplicating the ATCC vials already in liquid nitrogen. Cellosaurus lists 25+ provider catalog IDs for HeLa alone.

features.name: Owned-but-visible personal inventory ('My shelf') with sharing levels
features.description:
Every item or instance has an owner_id and a sharing_level:
- shared: anyone may use it
- ask_first (default): borrowing needs the owner's OK
- private_visible: the item and its owner always show in search, but quantity and location are hidden
- restricted: MTA or collaborator material, limited to named people
Each member gets a personal view. Lab-wide search always returns every level, so nobody can buy something the lab already owns without seeing it.
features.why_it_matters: People keep personal stock for rational reasons: worry about how others store and return reagents, contamination doubts, convenience. Forcing everything into a shared pool pushes stock back into hiding. Explicit but visible ownership removes the blind spot behind duplicate purchases without a political fight.
seen_in: LabCup (each lab keeps ownership; sharing by permission)
MIT lab shared-reagents sheet (personal stock may be contributed)

features.name: 'Who has this?' lookup and borrow/lend workflow
features.description: From a search result, 'Ask to borrow' sends a Slack/Teams DM to the owner with Approve/Decline buttons and the requested quantity. On approval the app records a transfer (from_owner, to_owner, qty, date, optional return-by date) and updates the instance. It sends return reminders and credits lenders on the leaderboard. There is also an 'Offer to lab' button for surplus and near-expiry items.
features.why_it_matters: Borrowing takes effort and can feel awkward (the AAAS piece calls it 'leg work'). A one-tap request makes borrowing easier than buying. Campus reuse programs show that visibility plus low-friction reuse saves real money.
seen_in: University of Michigan Lab Swap Shop

features.name: Open-requests board with stale-request cleanup
features.description: A lab-wide board, synced from Quartzy, of everything requested, approved, ordered or backordered, grouped by product, with requester, age, ETA and grant code. A nightly job flags anything ORDERED for more than 21 days without a receipt and DMs the requester 'Did this arrive?' with Received / Still waiting / Cancel buttons. The answer is written back to Quartzy.
features.why_it_matters: Seeing what is already on the way prevents the 'two people order the same thing the same week' case. Quartzy's duplicate warning keeps firing for stale Ordered requests until someone updates them, so cleanup keeps the alerts trustworthy.

features.name: Receiving-driven inventory creation with GS1 label scan
features.description: When a Quartzy request becomes RECEIVED (by webhook or nightly poll), or is received in the app, the app creates or merges an inventory instance from the order record: name, vendor, catalog, unit size, price, requester as default owner, spend_tracking_code. The receiver only confirms the location from a recent-locations picker. Optionally they scan the vendor's GS1 DataMatrix to fill lot (AI 10) and expiry (AI 17, YYMMDD), and print a QR label for item-level types. The app matches against existing products and items so stock is added rather than duplicated.
features.why_it_matters: Separate data entry is the main reason inventories go stale. Quartzy only offers 'add to existing item' when the request came from inventory or order history, so ad-hoc requests create duplicate inventory records. Doing it at receiving makes inventory a by-product of purchasing.
seen_in: Quartzy receive-and-add-to-inventory and mobile receiving (packing-slip photos)

features.name: One-tap point-of-use updates (scan -> big buttons)
features.description: A phone-camera web app, or a shared tablet at bench and freezer stations. Scanning an item or shelf QR shows large buttons: Used some, Running low, Empty, Moved, Discarded, plus 'use this one first' information. No typing, glove-friendly button sizes, and an offline queue that syncs later. Empty archives the instance; Running low triggers the reorder logic.
features.why_it_matters: When recording a withdrawal takes too many screens, staff write side notes and enter them later, or skip the system entirely. Accurate counts depend on capturing use at the moment it happens.
seen_in: Quartzy mobile app (scan, increase/reduce stock, request from the lab)
Thermo Fisher Supply Center 'scan and go' cabinets

features.name: Reorder points, par levels and de-duplicated auto-requests
features.description: Min/max levels per product per location. Suggested minimum = average weekly use x vendor lead time + safety stock, computed from usage events and Quartzy requested_at -> received timestamps. When stock falls below the minimum, the app creates one Quartzy request with POST /order-requests (requires lab_id, type_id, name, vendor_name, catalog_number, price, quantity), unless an open request already exists. Alternatively it pings the weekly supplies monitor. Standing-order templates cover high-volume consumables.
features.why_it_matters: Stock-outs push people into panic personal orders. Coordinated reordering prevents both the stock-out and the parallel purchase.
seen_in: Quartzy Min to Stock / Max to Stock + Auto-Request When Low (no new auto-request while one is New/Pending)

features.name: Shelf/bin kanban cards and rotating supplies monitor
features.description: Tips, gloves, tubes and media are not tracked box by box. Each shelf or bin gets a printed QR card (product, reorder quantity, vendor). Scanning it, or dropping it in a 'reorder' tray, means running low (the two-bin or last-box rule). A weekly rota with a Slack reminder and checklist assigns one member to check general supplies, as the RPI Dordick group does.
features.why_it_matters: Tracking every box of cheap consumables is wasted effort that kills adoption, and shelf-level signals capture most of the value. Quartzy's own training deck says barcodes are most useful where the same item is always kept.

features.name: FEFO pick guidance and expiry alerts
features.description: Search results list instances with the earliest expiry first and a 'use first' badge (first-expired-first-out). A weekly digest lists items expiring in 30/60/90 days with their value. Near-expiry items go on a 'use-me-first' shelf and are offered to labmates automatically. Discards are logged with a reason (expired, contaminated, unknown).
features.why_it_matters: Expired unused stock is money already lost, and it often hides a duplicate (two opened bottles of the same thing). First-in-first-out storage is standard advice.
seen_in: Quartzy item instances with expiration dates and reminders
Lab Manager inventory guide (FIFO, color-coded expiry labels)

features.name: Bulk import and de-dup wizard for legacy personal spreadsheets
features.description:
Upload an XLSX/CSV or link a Google Sheet. Steps:
1. Map columns, with saved templates.
2. Preview normalization.
3. Review clusters of likely duplicates (RapidFuzz token_set_ratio on name + catalog_key) and merge with one click.
Owner defaults to the uploader and sharing to ask_first. Only name and owner are required; rows without a location go to a 'needs location' queue. Quartzy order history can also be imported to seed the product master.
features.why_it_matters: The hidden personal inventories already exist as spreadsheets and notebooks. Letting people upload them as they are is the fastest way to make them visible, and users have long asked for Excel import of hundreds of reagents.
seen_in: Hacker News Quartzy user asking for import of 500+ reagents
Quartzy getting-started checklist: 'Upload your inventory (and order history)'

features.name: Slack/Teams bot: /have, duplicate DMs, arrivals, weekly digest
features.description:
- /have <query> returns holdings (owner, location, quantity) and open requests.
- DMs for duplicate warnings, borrow requests and arrivals (e.g. 'your anti-GFP arrived, 4C fridge B shelf 2').
- A Monday digest in #lab-inventory: arrivals, items expiring soon, low stock, stale requests, duplicates caught and $ avoided this month.
- Per-user settings (DMs vs digest only) to avoid notification fatigue.
features.why_it_matters: It meets people in the tool they already use instead of asking them to open another app. Quartzy's own Slack integration only covers order-status events.
seen_in: Quartzy Slack via webhooks + Workflow Builder (ordered/received; Shop shipped/delivered/backordered/canceled)
Labguru email to requester on arrival

features.name: Browser extension 'Already have it?' on vendor sites
features.description: A Chrome/Edge extension for product pages on Thermo Fisher, MilliporeSigma, ATCC, CST, Abcam, NEB and similar sites. It reads the catalog number from the URL, page content or embedded product data, calls the app API, and shows a banner such as 'Lab has 2 (Priya, -20C B2, exp 2027-03); Sam ordered 3 days ago', with Borrow / Join request / Continue to Quartzy Connect buttons.
features.why_it_matters: The buying decision is often made on vendor sites. Quartzy Connect (v2.6.2) and Labstep's extension create requests or items from vendor pages, but neither documents a check for existing stock. I found no reviewed product with this check, so it would be a differentiator.
seen_in: Quartzy Connect (creates requests, shows Quartzy quotes)
Labstep Chrome extension (adds vendor items to inventory)

features.name: Duplicate retrospective analyzer (baseline and savings report)
features.description: A notebook or scheduled job over 12-24 months of Quartzy order requests. It groups requests by normalized product or equivalence group and flags (a) the same product requested by different people within 30/60 days, and (b) purchases made while Quartzy inventory showed stock. It estimates the $ involved and lists the top item categories (not people). Re-run it monthly after launch to show the trend.
features.why_it_matters: The literature has no credible independent numbers on duplicate spend. The lab's own baseline is the most persuasive argument for the PI, and the only honest basis for claiming savings later.
seen_in: Lab Manager guidance: set post-go-live measures and baselines before go-live

features.name: PI dashboard and monthly one-page report
features.description:
Tiles:
- spend month-to-date and fiscal-year by grant (spend_tracking_code), project, person and vendor
- duplicates caught and $ avoided, counted conservatively (only accepted borrow/merge/cancel actions)
- borrow transfers
- value expiring in the next 90 days
- dead stock: value of items with no usage events in 12 months
- personal vs shared inventory value
- open requests by age
- data quality: % of items with owner + location
- adoption: weekly active users out of 30, % of updates captured at point of use
Exportable as CSV or PDF.
features.why_it_matters: The PI asked for visibility and money saved. Showing results at lab level rather than shaming individuals keeps everyone on board.
seen_in: Quartzy Spend Dashboard; monthly spend and weekly reconciliation emails

features.name: Spend and vendor analytics
features.description: Flags the same product bought from several vendors or at different prices, and price creep. Shows vendor lead times (requested_at -> received). Lists the top recurring items as candidates for standing orders or bulk deals, and spots group-buy opportunities when several people need the same thing.
features.why_it_matters: Consolidating recurring purchases is a commonly reported saving. One sponsored Lab Manager example reports 18% lower material costs after consolidating glove and media orders.

features.name: Stocktake / audit mode
features.description: A scan session, one location at a time: scan the location QR, then every item. Unscanned items go to a 'missing?' list sent to their owners. Items found but not listed can be quick-added. Progress is shown per bay, and stocktakes are scheduled quarterly with Slack reminders.
features.why_it_matters: Counts drift, and a short scheduled scan keeps people trusting the data. Warwick's mandatory LabCup stocktake with barcode scanners estimates 30-60 minutes for a small lab and 1-2 hours for a large research lab.

features.name: Inventory amnesty campaign with leaderboards
features.description: A time-boxed launch week. Points for items registered, locations verified, items shared or lent, duplicates averted and expired items discarded. A Slack leaderboard by bay or sub-team, small prizes, and a freezer clean-out at the same time.
features.why_it_matters: It makes entering the one-time backlog social and finite. The gamified Freezer Challenge drew 3,724 labs in 36 countries in 2025 and added leaderboards that year.
seen_in: My Green Lab / I2SL Freezer Challenge

features.name: Roles, rotator accounts, onboarding and offboarding
features.description:
Roles:
- PI: sees everything, approves above a threshold
- lab manager/admin
- member
- rotator/guest: account expires at the end of the rotation, requests need sponsor approval, and items they create belong to the sponsor by default
- viewer
Onboarding: a 10-minute task-based tour plus a 'first scan' checklist. Offboarding: the account can't be deactivated until the leaver's items are transferred, pooled or discarded.
features.why_it_matters: Turnover of students and postdocs is how knowledge and stock get orphaned. LEAF's toolkit explicitly includes induction and exit procedures.

features.name: Configurable lab policies and override reasons
features.description:
A rules engine:
- a reason is required to order despite a high-confidence match
- PI approval above $X
- purchases outside Quartzy (P-card, direct vendor, collaborator gifts) are logged through a 30-second form
- 'lab standard' products, as in the MIT lab rule: use the shared reagent rather than a similar one picked for personal preference
- a hint to order the smallest unit for personal-only items
features.why_it_matters: Clear rules the PI endorses are what make the software matter. The low-tech labs that keep duplicates under control rely on exactly these rules.
seen_in: Bitesize Bio single shared order list

features.name: Cell-line request guard
features.description: When a request looks like a cell line (vendor ATCC/ECACC/DSMZ/JCRB, or a name match), the app resolves it to a Cellosaurus accession. It shows the lab's liquid-nitrogen vials: passage, freeze date, mycoplasma and STR test dates, owner and MTA flag. It warns if the line is on the ICLAC register of misidentified cell lines (v14, Feb 2026, 608 lines).
features.why_it_matters: Cell lines are among the most expensive single duplicates (ATCC HeLa CCL-2 lists at $577 each), and misidentified lines are a recognized cost to reproducibility.
seen_in: ICLAC Register of Misidentified Cell Lines
Institutional cell-line repositories (UNC Lineberger, UC Berkeley)

features.name: Workaround register and in-app 'this is annoying' button
features.description: One tap logs a point of friction with context (screen, item, free text). Entries are triaged weekly, and the top 3 are fixed and announced. Adoption metrics are tracked against a baseline taken before launch.
features.why_it_matters: Workarounds are the earliest sign of failure and are effectively bug reports: spreadsheets reappearing, paper notes typed in later, one person doing all the entry.

features.name: Internal surplus marketplace (lab and neighbor labs)
features.description: Members list surplus or near-expiry items as free to claim, optionally visible to neighboring labs in the department. A claim creates a transfer. It can tie into campus swap shops where they exist.
features.why_it_matters: Campus reuse programs report large avoided costs: Michigan over $1M in under 2 years, UAB nearly $100k in 4 months, Caltech $200k+ (all self-reported).
seen_in: University of Michigan Lab Swap Shop

features.name: Group-buy / request merging
features.description: When two or more open needs match within a time window, the app suggests one combined order, or a larger pack size with a lower unit price, and splits the cost across spend_tracking_codes.
features.why_it_matters: It turns a would-be duplicate into a discount. My Green Lab advises coordinating with labmates on joint orders, and TCBE (Trinity College Dublin) pools purchases and bills each group by researcher count.
seen_in: Trinity College Dublin TCBE central ordering

key_insights: Quartzy's built-in duplicate guard is narrow (verified via its help-center text). It fires only when a new request has the same catalog # as a request in New, Approved, Ordered or Backordered status in the same Quartzy Lab. Received and Cancelled requests are ignored, inventory is never checked, and a stale 'Ordered' request keeps triggering the warning until someone updates it. Personal stock, other vendors, other pack sizes and members in different Quartzy Labs all slip through, which is the PI's exact problem.

Quartzy receiving can itself create duplicate records. When marking a request received you choose skip / create a new inventory item / add stock to an existing item, and the last option only appears if the request came from inventory or order history. Ad-hoc requests therefore keep spawning new inventory items unless something matches them to existing products.

Quartzy has the plumbing for a companion app:
- REST API at api.quartzy.com with an Access-Token header: /order-requests (GET/POST/PUT), /inventory-items (GET; quantity updates via PUT /inventory-items/{itemId}/instances/{instanceId}), /labs, /types, /user, /webhooks
- order requests carry requested_by, catalog_number, vendor_name, unit_price, spend_tracking_code and status (CREATED/APPROVED/ORDERED/BACKORDERED/RECEIVED/CANCELLED)
- webhooks are CloudEvents v1 with an HMAC-SHA256 'Signature' header, must get a 2xx within 3 s, and are retried 3 times (after 10, 100 and 1000 s)
- the current pricing page lists 'APIs and webhooks' as included

Licensing could leave members unable to see purchases. Quartzy's Academia plan is $50/month billed annually with 3 users included, and extra seat cost isn't stated. Since July 2023 academic labs pay per seat ($99-149 per seat per year at the time). In a 30-person lab many members may have no Quartzy access, and therefore no view of what is on order. A companion app could give everyone read access, but check Quartzy's terms first.

Duplicates are an identity problem as much as a visibility one. HeLa has 25+ provider catalog IDs in Cellosaurus (ATCC CCL-2, ECACC 93021013, DSMZ ACC-57, JCRB9004, RIKEN RCB0007 and more). Pack sizes, vendor rebrands and free-text names fragment the same product further. Matching on catalog number alone, which is Quartzy's approach, will miss many real duplicates.

Hidden personal inventories are rational. Commentary names trust in how others store and return reagents, doubt over whether a failed experiment came from a shared reagent, convenience, and hedging against shortages. One Yale lab kept up to 20 copies of a sample where 2-3 would do and bought chemicals it already had. Design for 'owned but visible', not confiscation.

Hard numbers on duplicate spending are scarce, and most quoted statistics are unsourced vendor marketing (Uncountable's 25%-of-hours and 45-min/day, Netguru's '2-5% of inventory tossed' and 'up to 97%', Best Lab Tech's '10-second rule'). The better evidence is self-reported but institutional:
- LEAF pilot: 235 lab groups, average GBP 3,700 per year saved, GBP 641k total; per UCL, about 23% came from more efficient use of research grants
- UCL Chemistry: up to GBP 90k per year from cataloguing 20,000 bottles in Quartzy and sharing them
- University of Michigan Lab Swap Shop: over $1M avoided in under 2 years
- UAB Green Marketplace: about $100k in 4 months
Measure the lab's own baseline from Quartzy history.

Adoption failure modes are well described (Lab Manager 2025-26 and older pieces):
- one superuser doing everyone's data entry ('not adoption')
- training only at go-live
- bench staff left out of design
- no system owner
- complicated interfaces that cause inconsistent entry
- spreadsheets and paper reappearing
Success patterns: superusers per area with protected time; training in three waves, with a follow-up 2-4 weeks after launch; a workaround register with the top 3 fixed visibly; metrics set before launch; never retiring the old method until the new one is faster.

Inventory has to be a by-product of purchasing and use, not a separate chore. Hacker News users called per-use logging of weigh-outs 'ludicrous'. Reviewers say Quartzy inventory needs manual updates, per-item status changes get cumbersome at 30+ orders a day, and one larger lab went back to a spreadsheet. Receiving-driven creation and scan-plus-big-buttons usage address exactly this.

Low-tech rules from real labs work and should be built into the app:
- MIT lab: shared-reagent sheet, 'stick to these reagents over something similar due to personal preference', a 'Running low?' column that notifies the orderer, and 'order the smallest possible unit' for non-shared items
- RPI Dordick group: weekly rotating supplies monitor, reorder from Quartzy inventory before taking the last box
- NMSU Chemical Engineering: the manager checks the requester's existing inventory before approving
- Bitesize Bio: one shared order list, an unclaimed-deliveries box, a monthly audit

Barcode strategy should be tiered. Use item-level labels for high-value or unique items (cell-line vials, antibodies, enzymes, kits) and shelf/bin-level codes for consumables; Quartzy's own deck says barcodes work best where the same item is always kept. Vendor GS1 DataMatrix labels (MilliporeSigma Smart Labels: AI 10 lot, AI 17 expiry YYMMDD) can be scanned at receiving to avoid typing.

I found no product that warns about already-owned items while you browse a vendor site. Quartzy Connect (v2.6.2, Oct 2026, about 495 users) and Labstep's Chrome extension only create requests or items. That makes an 'Already have it?' extension a genuine differentiator, though absence of evidence isn't proof it doesn't exist.

Time-boxed, gamified campaigns engage labs at scale. The 2025 Freezer Challenge had 3,724 labs in 36 countries, with points per action and new leaderboards. That fits a one-off 'inventory amnesty' to surface personal stock, followed by periodic stocktakes; Warwick estimates 30-60 minutes for a small lab with barcode scanners.

Academic context matters: labs are decentralized and constantly turning over. Dirnagl and Przesdzing advise offering a new system as an opportunity rather than forcing it, and found early users become 'avid supporters' who win over skeptics. They also warn that if the system becomes too complex, users record their work outside it. Offboarding (transferring a leaver's items) and onboarding for rotators are essential.

The reproducibility angle can help win support. Freedman et al. estimate about $28B per year of US preclinical research is irreproducible, and 15-36% of cell lines are misidentified. A cell-line guard (Cellosaurus ID, authentication dates, ICLAC warning) adds scientific value beyond saving money, which helps win over bench scientists.
recommendations:
Step 0 (week 0, PI and you): have the PI announce five rules at a lab meeting.
1. Every purchase goes through Quartzy, or is logged in the app within 24 h if it doesn't (P-card, direct vendor, collaborator gifts).
2. Search before you request; the app does the checking.
3. Personal stock is allowed but must be visible; the owner keeps control and the default is 'ask first'.
4. Ordering despite a strong duplicate match needs a one-line reason.
5. Everyone marks items received with a location.
Also name the roles: system owner (you), deputy (the other bioinformatician), operations owner (whoever approves Quartzy orders), and 3-4 bench champions, one per bay or sub-group, with a small explicit time allowance. Champions coach; they don't do other people's data entry.

Step 1 (week 1): measure before building. Pull 12-24 months of Quartzy order requests via the API (requested_by, catalog_number, vendor_name, item_name, quantity, unit_price, total_price, requested_at, status, spend_tracking_code) and current inventory. Normalize vendors and catalog numbers, cluster names, then count (a) the same product requested by different people within 30/60 days and (b) purchases made while stock was recorded. Show the PI the $ figure and the top item categories. Also record baseline adoption metrics: how many members can use Quartzy, % of requests created from inventory, % of received items with a location.

Step 2 (weeks 2-4): ship MVP 1, a visibility layer that needs no data entry:
- webhook sync plus a nightly reconciliation poll of Quartzy requests and inventory
- lab-wide search
- an open-requests board
- a Slack /have command
- real-time duplicate DMs to the requester and approver when a new Quartzy request matches stock or another open request
- stale-request nudges
Give all 30 members read access, after checking Quartzy's license terms.

Step 3 (weeks 3-5): test a prototype with 3-5 bench users doing real tasks: receive a package, take the last tube, find an antibody. Time each action against these targets: find 'who has X' in under 10 s, a point-of-use update in 2 taps after scanning, receiving in under 30 s. Cut required fields to name and owner, prompt for location, and make everything else optional or auto-filled.

Step 4 (weeks 5-6): run an 'Inventory Amnesty Week' to bring personal inventories into the open:
- members upload their spreadsheets through the import wizard (ownership kept, default 'ask first') or spend 30-60 minutes scanning a shelf or freezer with a champion
- label high-value items individually (cell-line vials, antibodies, enzymes, kits above a $ threshold)
- put shelf/bin QR cards on consumables
- run a points leaderboard with small prizes alongside a freezer clean-out
Promise no judgement about what turns up.

Step 5 (weeks 6-8): make receiving the way inventory enters the system. When a Quartzy request is RECEIVED, the app creates or merges the inventory instance from the order record. The receiver confirms the location, optionally scans the vendor GS1 code for lot and expiry, and prints a label; the default owner is the requester. From then on, new stock never needs separate data entry.

Step 6 (weeks 8-10): turn on checks at approval. The approver queue shows the duplicate panel with Merge / Decline-and-borrow / Approve buttons. Add the NMSU-style rule: if the requester already holds the product, they must give a reason. Mirror Quartzy's auto-approve price threshold so cheap consumables keep flowing.

Step 7 (weeks 8-12): usage and replenishment. Scanning shows Used / Low / Empty buttons, and Low creates a de-duplicated Quartzy request or pings the weekly supplies monitor (a rota like the RPI Dordick group's). Set min/max levels for the 30-50 highest-volume items and standing-order templates for gloves, tips and media.

Step 8 (weeks 10-14): sharing. Add borrow/lend DMs with transfer records, lender credit on the leaderboard, near-expiry 'free to good home' posts, and a curated lab-standard reagents list (MIT-style: use the shared item unless there is a scientific reason not to).

Train in waves, as Lab Manager recommends:
- wave 1: prototype sessions with bench staff
- wave 2: 15-minute task-based demos at the bench for each sub-group just before each feature goes live
- wave 3: a follow-up 2-4 weeks later to collect workarounds (the most valuable session and the one most often skipped)
Put a one-page cheat sheet and a QR code linking to the app at each bench and freezer.

First 90 days:
- in-person support at the bench for the first two weeks
- a 5-minute check-in at lab meeting weekly for a month
- a public workaround register, with the top 3 fixed and announced
- old spreadsheets kept read-only until the app is clearly faster
Watch for warning signs: spreadsheets reappearing, entries batched at the end of the day, one person doing most of the entries.

Reporting: a Monday Slack digest (arrivals, items expiring within 30 days, low stock, stale requests, duplicates caught and $ avoided). A monthly one-page PI report: spend by grant, project and vendor; duplicates avoided, counted conservatively; expiring and dead-stock value; personal vs shared value; adoption metrics. Keep per-person views for the PI and lab manager only, and celebrate lenders rather than naming 'duplicators'.

Keep it going:
- build the app into onboarding for every rotator and new member (a 10-minute task tour plus a first scan)
- build it into offboarding: an account can't be closed until its items are transferred, pooled or discarded
- a 1-hour quarterly stocktake, scanning by location
- an annual freezer clean-out (join the Freezer Challenge or LEAF if your institution participates)
- re-run the duplicate analyzer monthly and show the trend

Ambitious phase, once adoption is stable:
- the 'Already have it?' browser extension for vendor sites
- equivalence groups based on Cellosaurus, RRID and CAS identifiers
- a cell-line guard with the ICLAC check
- group-buy merging
- opt-in sharing with neighboring labs
- LEAF-style savings reporting

Architecture guardrails:
- keep Quartzy as the place purchases are made; don't build a competing order form that bypasses its approvals
- the app owns visibility, duplicate checks, personal stock, usage tracking and sharing
- use a plain, well-documented Python stack and keep all data exportable (only two bioinformaticians can maintain it)
- if possible, use an access token from a dedicated service account rather than a person's account
- handle webhooks with a fast 2xx, a work queue, and nightly reconciliation

tech_components.need: Two-way integration with Quartzy (requests, inventory, receiving events)
tech_components.recommended: Quartzy REST API (api.quartzy.com, Access-Token header) plus webhooks, with a nightly reconciliation poll
tech_components.rationale: Keeps Quartzy as the place purchases are made while the app adds visibility and duplicate checks. The pricing page lists APIs and webhooks as included.
alternatives: CSV exports from Quartzy (no real time)
gotchas: Webhooks expect a 2xx within 3 s and retry only 3 times (after 10, 100 and 1000 s): acknowledge fast, queue the work, reconcile nightly
Verify the HMAC-SHA256 'Signature' header with the secret shown once at creation; webhooks are configured in Lab Settings > Developer
Exact order-request event type strings aren't fully documented ('inventory-item.updated' and com.quartzy.sales-order-item.* are confirmed)
Use lab.uses_instances logic and instance endpoints; parent-level lot/expiry/location fields are deprecated
Access tokens are per user, so a token tied to a person who leaves breaks the integration; I didn't confirm which roles may set APPROVED/CANCELLED via the API
Check Quartzy's terms before showing Quartzy data to members without seats

tech_components.recommended: Tiered matcher: exact normalized keys and external identifiers first; then PostgreSQL pg_trgm candidate retrieval (GIN gin_trgm_ops index); then RapidFuzz scoring with item-type-specific rules
tech_components.rationale: pg_trgm gives fast fuzzy lookups inside the database (default similarity_threshold 0.3, word_similarity_threshold 0.6). RapidFuzz (MIT) gives tunable scores (token_set_ratio, WRatio) for ranking and for clustering during import.
gotchas: Near-identical strings can be different products (anti-GFP vs anti-RFP, different conjugates, hosts or pack sizes); add negative rules and require override reasons only for high-confidence matches
Calibrate thresholds on 12-24 months of Quartzy history and keep a 'not a duplicate' feedback loop
Normalization rules for vendor catalog suffixes need per-vendor testing (not verified here)

tech_components.need: Capture lot and expiry at receiving without typing
tech_components.recommended: biip (Python, Apache-2.0) to parse GS1 element strings and GS1 Digital Link from vendor DataMatrix/QR codes; decode with the phone camera in the web app
tech_components.rationale: Vendors such as MilliporeSigma encode lot (AI 10) and expiry (AI 17, YYMMDD) in GS1 labels, which removes the most error-prone typing at receiving.
alternatives: Dedicated USB/Bluetooth 2D scanners at the receiving bench
gotchas: Variable-length fields (lot, serial) rely on FNC1 separators that some decoders drop
Label formats vary by vendor; Thermo Fisher's format wasn't verified here; test with real labels

tech_components.need: Chat bot, DMs and weekly digest
tech_components.recommended: Slack Bolt for Python (or a Microsoft Teams bot if the lab uses Teams)
tech_components.rationale: Official framework; supports slash commands (/have), interactive Approve/Decline buttons for borrow requests and duplicate prompts, and scheduled digests. Quartzy's own Slack workflows only cover order-status events.
alternatives: Quartzy's Slack Workflow Builder integration (order events only)
gotchas: A workspace admin may need to approve the app
Respect per-user notification preferences to avoid fatigue (reviewers complain about Quartzy email volume)
Socket Mode vs a public HTTP endpoint wasn't verified in this session

tech_components.need: Identifier enrichment for cross-vendor equivalence and the cell-line guard
tech_components.recommended: Cellosaurus accessions for cell lines plus the ICLAC register (Excel, v14) for misidentification warnings; RRIDs for antibodies; CAS/PubChem for chemicals
tech_components.rationale: One accession groups many provider catalog numbers (HeLa: ATCC CCL-2, ECACC 93021013, DSMZ ACC-57, JCRB9004, RIKEN RCB0007 and more), which catalog matching can't do.
gotchas: Antibody Registry and PubChem access couldn't be verified in this session
Cache identifiers locally and let the lab manager override mappings

pitfalls: Building a parallel ordering flow that bypasses Quartzy approvals creates two sources of truth. Keep Quartzy for purchasing and let the app do visibility, checks, usage and sharing.

False-positive duplicate alerts cause alert fatigue (e.g. anti-GFP vs anti-RFP, different conjugates or pack sizes). Ask for a reason only on high-confidence matches, make 'not a duplicate' a one-tap answer, and tune on history.
Stale Quartzy requests ('Ordered' for months) poison duplicate checks and Quartzy's own warning. Automate the 'did this arrive?' nudges.
Forcing personal stock into a shared pool, or making 'private' invisible, drives stock back into hiding. Make ownership explicit but always visible.
Too many required fields, or tracking every box of cheap consumables, is the classic way inventories die. Require only name and owner; use shelf-level cards for consumables.
The superuser trap: if the lab manager or a bioinformatician becomes everyone's data-entry clerk, usage stats look healthy while the system depends on one person.
Training once at go-live and skipping the follow-up 2-4 weeks later, which is where workarounds surface.
Retiring the old spreadsheets before the app is clearly faster, or ignoring warning signs: spreadsheets reappearing, entries batched at the end of the day.
Per-person dashboards used to shame people lead to gaming and hiding. Report at lab level, celebrate lenders, and keep individual views for the PI and lab manager.
Quoting unsourced vendor statistics to the PI (25% of time, 2-5% waste, 97% time cut, 10-second rule). Measure the lab's own baseline and count savings conservatively.
Webhook fragility: a 3 s timeout and only 3 retries means missed events unless you queue and reconcile nightly. Quartzy's instances migration and deprecated fields can break naive code.
Seat licensing: members without Quartzy seats may have no visibility, and showing Quartzy data to them may raise license questions. Confirm with Quartzy.
Bus factor for a two-person bioinformatics team. Use a plain, documented stack, keep data exportable, use a service-account token, and avoid clever infrastructure.
Bench realities: gloves, BSL-2 areas where phones are discouraged, frost on -80C and liquid-nitrogen labels. Put shared tablets or scanners at stations, use large buttons, and use cryo-rated labels.
MTA or collaborator materials and unpublished reagents must not be auto-shared. Provide a 'restricted' sharing level.
open_questions: Who approves and places Quartzy orders today: a dedicated lab manager, the PI, or each member? Is approval required for every request or only above a $ threshold?
How many Quartzy 'Labs' does the group use, how many of the 30 people have Quartzy seats, and which plan or organizational license do you have? Quartzy's duplicate check works only within one Lab.
Can you get a Quartzy API token, ideally for a service account, and set up webhooks (Lab Settings > Developer)? Who is Lab Admin?
Roughly what share of purchases bypass Quartzy (P-card, direct vendor sites, core facilities, collaborator gifts)?
Which categories drive the duplicate cost: cell lines, antibodies, kits, enzymes, media/FBS, consumables? Any recent examples to calibrate the matcher?
Does the lab use Slack, Microsoft Teams, or only email?
Hosting and identity constraints: university IT policies, single sign-on (Shibboleth/SAML/Azure AD), whether you can run a small VM or must use approved cloud?
Are personal inventories funded by individual fellowships or grants, which affects sharing politics? Will the PI mandate visibility and reasons for overriding duplicate warnings?
Are phones allowed at the bench and in BSL-2 rooms? Is there a label printer (and cryo labels) and budget for a few 2D scanners or tablets?
How many personal spreadsheets or freezer maps exist today, and is there one shared one?
Does the PI want per-person spend views or lab-level only? Should neighboring labs or the department be in scope later?
Does your institution run LEAF, My Green Lab, the Freezer Challenge or a lab swap shop that the rollout could align with?

research.angle: tech: technical building blocks for a self-hosted internal web app maintained by one Python-literate bioinformatician, used by about 30 people on desktops and on phones at the bench
research.summary:
The lowest-risk stack for one maintainer is a plain Python monolith. Use Django 6.1 now and move to Django 6.2 LTS when it ships in April 2027 (supported until April 2030). Add PostgreSQL 18, which is supported until November 2030. For pages, use server-rendered templates with htmx 2.0.x and Alpine.js. Django admin works as the lab manager's back office, and one small JS module handles camera scanning. Django 6.0 added three useful built-ins: template partials (a natural fit for htmx), built-in CSP, and a Tasks API. InvenTree, a mature open-source inventory system, uses the same backend pattern: Django API-first, Django-Q2 workers, and Gunicorn behind Caddy.

Stopping duplicate orders needs two things. First, every product needs one identity: vendor family + normalized catalog number + GTIN, with pg_trgm fuzzy matching as a fallback. Second, the app needs a live copy of Quartzy order requests. Quartzy's public API covers this (verified: GET/POST/PUT /order-requests with statuses CREATED/APPROVED/ORDERED/RECEIVED/CANCELLED/BACKORDERED, /inventory-items, /webhooks).

Getting bench scientists to use it depends on scanning. iOS Safari still ships BarcodeDetector disabled by default (through iOS 27.2). html5-qrcode and zxing-js are both in maintenance mode, and quagga2 reads only 1D codes. So use barcode-detector backed by zxing-wasm, and parse vendor codes with biip 5.2.0. MilliporeSigma prints GS1 DataMatrix (AIs 01/10/17/21). NEB uses its own Code 128 format (catalog #, lot, YYMM assay date, YYMM expiry). I could not confirm Thermo Fisher, Bio-Rad, Corning or QIAGEN practice.

For labels, use two printers. A Brother QL on the network, driven by brother_ql_next, handles boxes and bottles. A Zebra thermal-transfer printer with 8000T CryoCool labels (rated to −196 °C, ZPL sent over port 9100) handles cryovials. Brady B-490/B-461 media is also rated to −196 °C. Avoid DYMO 550/5XL printers: they only accept DYMO's RFID-chipped label rolls.

Other choices:
- Login: django-allauth 65.21.0 (SAML/OIDC, login-by-code, passkeys).
- Messages: a Slack app using Bolt Socket Mode, which works behind a campus firewall, or Teams Workflows webhooks. Office 365 connectors stopped working May 18–22, 2026.
- Background jobs and schedules: Django-Q2 1.11.1.
- History: an append-only stock ledger plus django-simple-history 3.13.
- Backups: nightly pg_dump + restic 0.19.1.

Hosting costs €6–$25 a month, or nothing on a university VM.

Claude API features are cheap per call:
- Label photo: about $0.0004 on Haiku 5.5, $0.008 on Sonnet 5.5, $0.02–0.03 on Opus 5.5.
- 12-page SDS: about $0.006 / $0.11 / $0.23 on the same three models, half that with the Batch API.

So cost is not what limits AI here; accuracy and a human confirming each result are.

Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through. GS1 practice at Thermo Fisher, Bio-Rad, Corning and QIAGEN, Render pricing, camera behaviour in iOS home-screen apps, and how keyboard-wedge scanners handle GS1 codes were not verified. Points marked as inference come from my own reasoning, not a source.

features.name: Scan-first mobile item page (installable PWA)
features.description: Scanning a lab-printed QR/DataMatrix (phone camera via barcode-detector/zxing-wasm, or a keyboard-wedge scanner) opens the container record with 3-4 large actions: Use some / Mark empty / Move / Reorder. Quantity changes use +/- steppers and presets (full, ~half, low, empty) instead of typing. URL-style payloads (https://inv.<lab>/i/7F3K9Q) also open from the native camera app.
features.why_it_matters: Bench users wearing gloves won't type. Updating stock has to take seconds, or the data goes stale and nobody trusts the duplicate check.

features.name: Receive-by-scan with GS1 auto-fill
features.description: At the receiving bench, scan the vendor barcode. biip parses GTIN (01), lot (10), expiry (17) and serial (21) from GS1-128/DataMatrix. Vendor-specific parsers handle non-GS1 formats such as NEB's Code 128 (catalog #, 8-digit lot, YYMM assay date, YYMM expiry). The item is matched to the open Quartzy order request by vendor + catalog #. One flow creates the container record(s), assigns a location and prints labels.
features.why_it_matters: No hand-typed lot/expiry. Receipt is tied to the order, which closes the 'has it arrived?' gap that leads to re-ordering.

features.name: 'Already have it?' pre-order duplicate check
features.description: Before a request is created (in-app form, pasted catalog # or vendor URL), the matcher searches three places: on-hand containers including declared personal stock, open Quartzy order requests (CREATED/APPROVED/ORDERED/BACKORDERED), and recent receipts. Matching runs exact GTIN -> exact normalized catalog # -> same base catalog # with a different pack size -> trigram name similarity within the vendor family -> confirmed cross-vendor equivalents. The result shows who has it, where, how much, and whether a colleague already requested it. The user can still continue with a one-line reason (soft block).
features.why_it_matters: Goes straight at the PI's double-order problem. A soft block avoids pushing people back to ordering outside the system.
seen_in: Quartzy order-request data model (statuses, requested_by, catalog_number)

features.name: Quartzy sync and bridge
features.description: A worker job polls GET /order-requests (per lab_id, paginated) about every 10 minutes and/or registers POST /webhooks. It mirrors status, requester, vendor_name, catalog_number, quantity, unit_size, total_price and spend_tracking_code. Optionally, the app creates requests itself via POST /order-requests (needs lab_id, type_id, name, vendor_name, catalog_number, price, quantity), so the duplicate check runs in front of Quartzy. A RECEIVED status creates a 'to receive and label' task.
features.why_it_matters: Quartzy stays the purchasing system of record, and the app always knows what is already being ordered.

features.name: Canonical product catalog with normalized catalog numbers
features.description: Product table keyed by (vendor_family, catalog_base) with pack-specific catalog_norm, many GTINs per product, a vendor alias table (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich/MilliporeSigma/Merck/Supelco in one family; Thermo Fisher/Invitrogen/Gibco/Applied Biosystems in another), and separate manufacturer catalog # vs distributor SKU. A unique B-tree index sits on the normalized key.
features.why_it_matters: Without one identity per product, the same reagent shows up under different spellings and duplicates slip through.

features.name: Cross-vendor equivalents (substitute groups)
features.description: Lab-manager-curated equivalence groups (e.g., the same medium or enzyme from two vendors). Candidates are suggested by trigram similarity and, optionally, a Claude re-ranker, then confirmed by a person. The duplicate check also flags equivalents ('we have the Corning version').
features.why_it_matters: Many duplicate orders are the same thing from a different vendor, not the identical SKU.

features.name: Declared personal stock with lab-wide visibility
features.description: Every container has an owner and a visibility level: lab-visible by default, a 'reserved for my experiment' flag instead of hiding it, and 'restricted' only for regulated items. django-rules predicates let owners and managers edit, while everyone can see that the item exists and where it is.
features.why_it_matters: Personal inventories are the root cause the PI named. 'Reserved but visible' keeps ownership while still preventing a re-order.

features.name: Hierarchical locations and freezer box maps
features.description: Room -> freezer/fridge/LN2 dewar -> shelf/rack -> box -> grid position (9x9, 10x10, configurable). Each level has a QR label. Containers are placed by scanning the box, then tapping a slot. The box view highlights empty and expiring slots, and a move is two scans.
features.why_it_matters: 'Where is it?' is the second most common question after 'do we have it?'. Cell lines and aliquots are useless if they can't be found.

features.name: One-click label printing service
features.description: Print queue with printer profiles: Brother QL raster over TCP (brother_ql_next), Zebra ZPL over raw TCP 9100, and PDF label sheets for browser printing (e.g., LabTAG laser cryo sheets). Includes templates per item type, reprint, a ZPL preview, and an optional local print agent (Raspberry Pi) that polls the server when the server can't reach printers directly.
features.why_it_matters: Labels with a scannable ID are what make every later scan workflow possible. Printing must be one tap at receiving.

features.name: Append-only stock ledger plus change history
features.description: Every quantity or location change is a StockTransaction row (receive, open, consume, aliquot/split, transfer, adjust, dispose) with user, timestamp, client UUID and reason. Current quantity is derived or cached from the ledger. django-simple-history records who changed reference data (product, cell-line metadata).
features.why_it_matters: Trustworthy numbers and an answer to 'who used the last vial?'. Offline scans can be replayed safely in order.

features.name: Low-stock, expiry and stale-record alerts with weekly digest
features.description: Scheduled jobs (Django-Q2 schedules) flag items below a reorder threshold, items expiring within N days (handling YYMMDD with DD=00 and NEB-style YYMM), and containers not touched in 12 months. Results go out as a weekly email/Slack digest per owner and a lab-manager summary.
features.why_it_matters: Reordering ahead of need, together with visibility, removes the panic orders that create duplicates.

features.name: Interactive Slack or Teams nudges
features.description: For example: 'Ana requested Lipofectamine 3000; 2 unopened in Freezer B / Shelf 3 (owner: Raj)' with buttons [View] [Cancel my request] [Order anyway]. Built with Slack Bolt for Python in Socket Mode (no public Request URL needed), or Teams Workflows webhooks with Adaptive Cards (posting only; interactive Teams needs a bot).
features.why_it_matters: Catches duplicates where people already talk. A one-tap cancel is what actually saves the money.

features.name: University SSO and passwordless phone login
features.description: django-allauth with SAML 2.0 (university IdP) or OIDC (Microsoft Entra/Google), plus login-by-code (ACCOUNT_LOGIN_BY_CODE_ENABLED; 180 s code, 3 attempts) and passkeys (MFA_SUPPORTED_TYPES += 'webauthn', MFA_PASSKEY_LOGIN_ENABLED) for quick phone sign-in. Long sessions on personal phones; MFA required for admins.
features.why_it_matters: Every password prompt at the bench costs adoption. SSO also removes accounts automatically when people leave.

features.name: Roles and object-level permissions
features.description: Django Groups for Member / Lab manager (purchasing) / PI / Admin, plus django-rules predicates such as is_owner, is_manager and is_restricted_item for edit/dispose/move rights. Read access is broad by default.
features.why_it_matters: Lets the lab be open by default while protecting regulated or precious items. Keeps the policy in code instead of per-row grants.

features.name: Bulk import of personal spreadsheets and Quartzy inventory, with dedupe preview
features.description: django-import-export admin import with a dry-run preview and column mapping. Catalog columns are imported as text; each row runs through the normalization and duplicate matcher, and suggested merges are shown before commit. Export to CSV/XLSX is available for the PI and EHS.
features.why_it_matters: Getting the 30 hidden personal inventories in on day one is the fastest way to show value and expose duplicates.

features.name: Typo-tolerant global search
features.description: Search-as-you-type (htmx) across name, synonyms, catalog #, CAS #, lot, owner and location. Runs Postgres full-text search (SearchVectorField + GIN, websearch syntax) plus pg_trgm word similarity for typos. Results are grouped by product with on-hand counts.
features.why_it_matters: If searching is slower than walking to the freezer, nobody searches before ordering.

features.name: Offline scan queue for cold rooms and basements
features.description: The service worker caches the app shell and location/box maps. Scans and ledger events made offline are stored in IndexedDB with client UUIDs and replayed when the app is opened or the 'online' event fires (Background Sync is not available in Safari or Firefox). Shows a 'N pending' badge and calls navigator.storage.persist().
features.why_it_matters: Cold rooms and basement freezers often have dead Wi-Fi. A failed scan teaches people not to bother.

features.name: Cell line registry with cryo vial tracking
features.description: A cell line record (Cellosaurus/RRID, source, MTA, BSL, mycoplasma and STR test dates) linked to vial-level containers (passage, freeze date, frozen by, box position) with thaw and freeze events in the ledger. Alerts when no authentication record exists or when the last vial of a line is used.
features.why_it_matters: Cell lines are a named duplicate-purchase item, and losing the last vial is costly.

features.name: Antibody registry with RRID and validated dilutions
features.description: Antibody records (target, clone, host, isotype, conjugate, RRID, vendor/catalog, lot) with per-application validated dilutions and notes, plus aliquot containers.
features.why_it_matters: Antibodies are expensive and often bought again because nobody knows a validated one is already in someone's box.

features.name: Plasmid and strain registry with sequence files
features.description: Upload GenBank/SnapGene/FASTA files. Metadata such as length, features and resistance markers is parsed server-side (Biopython, inference). Records link glycerol stocks and DNA preps as containers with locations, plus Addgene ID, MTA and biosafety notes.
features.why_it_matters: Stops people re-requesting or re-cloning constructs the lab already has. The bioinformatician can maintain this part easily.

features.name: SDS library with hazard extraction
features.description: SDS PDFs stored per product and revision (SHA-256 dedupe). A Claude PDF job (Batch API at night) extracts the signal word, GHS pictograms, H/P statements, storage class, flash point and CAS into structured fields that a person reviews before saving. Produces storage-segregation warnings and a hazardous inventory export for EHS.
features.why_it_matters: Safety/compliance visibility. Also gives the PI a reason to keep chemical inventory centralized.

features.name: AI photo intake for labels and packing slips
features.description: Snap a photo of a label, packing slip or handwritten tube. The client crops and resizes the image, Claude vision returns JSON (vendor, catalog #, lot, expiry, quantity, confidence) via structured outputs, and a prefilled form highlights low-confidence fields for a person to confirm. Used when no barcode parses.
features.why_it_matters: Covers vendors without GS1 codes and legacy personal stock, without typing.

features.name: Natural-language inventory assistant
features.description: 'Do we have Q5 polymerase, and where?' / 'Which cell lines haven't had a mycoplasma test in 6 months?'. Claude tool use over read-only, permission-scoped query functions (search_products, list_containers, open_requests), never raw SQL. Answers link to records.
features.why_it_matters: Lowers the barrier for wet-lab members who don't learn UIs. Optional delight feature.

features.name: Savings and spend dashboard
features.description: Counts duplicate warnings that led to cancelled requests, multiplied by Quartzy unit_price ('$ avoided'). Also spend by spend_tracking_code/type/vendor over time, top duplicate-prone items, and the fraction of stock that is declared and scanned.
features.why_it_matters: Gives the PI evidence that the tool pays off, which keeps people using it.

features.name: Automation API and outbound webhooks
features.description: A django-ninja JSON API with OpenAPI docs, used for the scanner/print agent, the Quartzy webhook receiver, AI jobs, and scripts by the bioinformatics team (e.g., an ELN link or bulk updates).
features.why_it_matters: Keeps the bioinformatician productive and lets the system grow without changing the UI.

features.name: Automated backups, restore drills and uptime monitoring
features.description: Nightly pg_dump -Fc plus media files, sent to off-site storage with restic (retention policy). A monthly scripted restore into a scratch database. Heartbeat monitors on backup and sync jobs, error tracking, and an admin status page.
features.why_it_matters: With a single maintainer, a silent backup failure or outage would destroy trust in the system.

products.name: InvenTree
products.stack: Django backend (API-first) + React/Mantine SPA (Vite) served as static files; 'Q2' (Django-Q2) worker processes with a database-backed task queue; Gunicorn behind Caddy/Nginx/Apache; optional Redis cache
standout_features: inventree-brother-plugin for Brother QL/PT network printing
Stock locations and mobile companion app
strengths: A real-world reference for the exact Django + Django-Q2 + Caddy pattern recommended here
Label printing and barcode plugins already exist
Mature permissions and REST API
weaknesses: Designed for electronics and manufacturing parts (suppliers, BOMs), not cell lines, antibodies or plasmids
No Quartzy integration
React SPA means a second (JS) codebase if you fork it
products.fit_notes: Use it as a reference design. You could prototype on it for a week, but a fork would need significant biology-specific work. Taking ideas from its plugin and printing design is cheaper than inheriting its codebase.
products.license_or_pricing: Open source (license not verified in this session)

products.name: Quartzy public API
products.stack: REST, base https://api.quartzy.com, Access-Token header (token from app.quartzy.com/profile/access-tokens)
products.activity: Live; PUT /inventory-items/{id} marked deprecated in favour of instance-level updates
standout_features: GET/POST/PUT /order-requests with statuses CREATED, APPROVED, ORDERED, RECEIVED, CANCELLED, BACKORDERED
Order request fields incl. vendor_name, catalog_number, item_name, unit_size, unit_price, total_price, requested_by, requested_at, spend_tracking_code, is_urgent
strengths: Has everything a duplicate check needs: what is requested, by whom, and its status
The app can create requests, so the check can run in front of Quartzy
weaknesses: Webhook event-type values, rate limits and page size are not documented on the API page
Token is per user, so a service account or token ownership has to be decided
products.fit_notes: The integration that matters most. Start with polling every ~10 min and add webhooks once you know the event types.
products.license_or_pricing: Included with Quartzy (plan-level API availability not verified)

products.name: barcode-detector + zxing-wasm
products.stack: JS/TS ESM; ZXing-C++ compiled to WebAssembly
products.activity: Active (npm 3.x line; zxing-wasm maintained by the same author)
standout_features: Spec-compatible BarcodeDetector ponyfill/polyfill (uses native when present)
Formats: qr_code incl. micro/rMQR, data_matrix, code_128, ean_13, itf, databar, pdf417, aztec; shorthands gs1_codes, any
strengths: Works on iOS Safari, where native BarcodeDetector is disabled
GS1-aware decoding (zxing-wasm marks GS1 support for DataMatrix/QR/Code 128/DataBar)
MIT license
weaknesses: ~1.04 MiB reader-only WASM (~1.46 MiB full) to download and cache
Speed on older iPhones not verified
products.fit_notes: Recommended in-browser scanner.
products.license_or_pricing: MIT (bundles Apache-2.0 zxing-cpp and BSD-3 zint)

products.name: html5-qrcode
products.activity: README: 'maintenance mode until further notice'; no bug fixes, PRs not merged
strengths: Easy to start with; many tutorials
weaknesses: Unmaintained
Built on zxing-js, which is itself in maintenance mode
BarcodeDetector integration is experimental
products.fit_notes: Avoid for new work.

products.name: quagga2
products.activity: Maintained as an interim fork 'until... replaced by built-in browser functionality'
standout_features: 1D symbologies: EAN, Code 128, Code 39, UPC, I2of5, Codabar, Code 93
strengths: Good for 1D-only retail codes
weaknesses: No DataMatrix; QR only via a separate sample reader
products.fit_notes: Not suitable as the main scanner, since lab labels and GS1 vendor codes are 2D.

products.name: biip
standout_features: GTIN-8/12/13/14, GS1 AI element strings (fixed and variable length, configurable separator)
Symbology identifier detection selects the parser automatically
Dates -> datetime with day '00' = last day of month; HRI output
strengths: Purpose-built and actively maintained
Pure Python
weaknesses: Handles GS1 only; vendor-specific formats (e.g., NEB Code 128) need your own parsers
products.fit_notes: First parser in the receive-by-scan chain.

products.name: brother_ql_next
products.stack: Python >=3.9; implements Brother QL raster language
products.activity: 0.12.0 released 2026-05-20; upstream pklaus/brother_ql described as unmaintained (last 0.9.4, 2019)
